claim: Respiratory complex I is a proton-pumping oxidoreductase key to bioenergetic metabolism.
source: Respiratory complex I is a proton-pumping oxidoreductase key to bioenergetic metabolism.
evidence: This is a general statement about complex I function that is established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Complex I from Deuterostomia including mammals can adopt a biochemically defined off-pathway 'deactive' state.
source: Complex I from Deuterostomia including mammals can adopt a biochemically defined off-pathway 'deactive' state, whereas complex I from Protostomia cannot.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous biochemical studies and is a key premise of the manuscript.

claim: Complex I from Protostomia cannot adopt a biochemically defined off-pathway 'deactive' state.
source: Complex I from Deuterostomia including mammals can adopt a biochemically defined off-pathway 'deactive' state, whereas complex I from Protostomia cannot.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous biochemical studies (Maklashina et al., 2003) and is a key premise of the manuscript.

claim: D. melanogaster complex I (Dm-CI) does not have a NEM-sensitive deactive state.
source: We show that although D. melanogaster complex I (Dm-CI) does not have a NEM-sensitive deactive state, it does show slow activation kinetics indicative of an off-pathway resting state.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1B and related activity assays.

claim: D. melanogaster complex I shows slow activation kinetics indicative of an off-pathway resting state.
source: We show that although D. melanogaster complex I (Dm-CI) does not have a NEM-sensitive deactive state, it does show slow activation kinetics indicative of an off-pathway resting state.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1E and G showing activation lag phases.

claim: The resting-state structure of Dm-CI from the thoracic muscle reveals multiple conformations.
source: The resting-state structure of Dm-CI from the thoracic muscle reveals multiple conformations.
evidence: This claim is supported by cryoEM structural data showing different conformational states.

claim: An N-terminal α-helix on the NDUFS4 subunit wedges between the peripheral and membrane arms in a helix-locked state.
source: We identify a helix-locked state in which an N-terminal α-helix on the NDUFS4 subunit wedges between the peripheral and membrane arms.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4A and related structural analysis.

claim: The Dm-CI off-pathway resting state is NEM insensitive.
source: Comparison of the Dm-CI structure and conformational states to those observed in bacteria, yeast, and mammals provides insight into the roles of subunits across organisms, explains why the Dm-CI off-pathway resting state is NEM insensitive, and raises questions regarding current mechanistic models of complex I turnover.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B and structural analysis explaining the molecular basis.

claim: CI couples the transfer of electrons from NADH to CoQ to the pumping of four H+ across the IMM.
source: CI couples the transfer of electrons from NADH to CoQ to the pumping of four H+ across the IMM (Galkin et al., 1999; Jones et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies establishing this stoichiometry.

claim: Complex I has an 'L' shaped structure consisting of a peripheral arm and a membrane arm.
source: It has an 'L' shaped structure consisting of two arms: a peripheral arm (PA) that extends into the matrix and a membrane arm (MA) that is embedded in the IMM.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about complex I architecture.

claim: The catalytic core of 14 subunits is conserved across species with few exceptions.
source: With few exceptions, the catalytic core of 14 subunits is conserved across species and contains all the redox cofactors and active sites required for catalysis (Hirst, 2013; Sazanov, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles summarizing structural conservation.

claim: Eukaryotic CI has varying numbers of accessory subunits, e.g., 29 in the yeast Yarrowia lipolytica and 31 in mammals.
source: In addition to the core subunits, eukaryotic CI has varying numbers of accessory subunits, e.g., 29 in the yeast Yarrowia lipolytica and 31 in mammals (Carroll et al., 2003; Letts and Sazanov, 2015; Padavannil et al., 2021; Parey et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Accessory subunits are needed for the assembly and stability of the complex.
source: The accessory subunits are needed for the assembly and stability of the complex (Garcia et al., 2017; Stroud et al., 2016) and in some cases may play an active role in regulating turnover (Padavannil et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Resting CI from yeast and mammals exist in two distinct biochemical states: the catalytically competent active (A) state and the off-pathway deactive (D) state.
source: Complicating the structural elucidation of the coupling mechanism is the fact that resting CI from yeast and mammals used for detailed structural studies have been shown to exist in two distinct biochemical states: the catalytically competent active (A) state and the off-pathway deactive (D) state (Gavrikova and Vinogradov, 1999; Maklashina et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous biochemical studies.

claim: CI spontaneously undergoes an A-to-D transition when exposed to physiological temperatures in the absence of reduced substrates in yeast and mammals.
source: In these species, CI spontaneously undergoes an A-to-D transition when exposed to physiological temperatures in the absence of reduced substrates (Babot et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous biochemical study.

claim: The D state is characterized by a solvent-exposed cysteine residue on the transmembrane helix 1–2 loop of the ND3 core subunit (TMH1-2ND3) that can be modified by thiol-reactive agents such as N-ethyl maleimide (NEM).
source: Biochemically, the D state is characterized by a solvent-exposed cysteine residue on the transmembrane helix 1–2 loop of the ND3 core subunit (TMH1-2ND3) that can be modified by thiol-reactive agents such as N-ethyl maleimide (NEM) (Galkin et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous biochemical study.

claim: Modification of the cysteine residue traps CI in the D state.
source: Modification of the cysteine residue traps CI in the D state.
evidence: This claim is supported by established biochemical knowledge about NEM modification.

claim: The presence of the D state is thought to protect cells from ROS-mediated damage due to CI reverse electron transport.
source: The presence of the D state is thought to protect cells from ROS-mediated damage due to CI reverse electron transport (Chouchani et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study proposing this protective function.

claim: The A-to-D transition is not universally conserved across species.
source: Nonetheless, the A-to-D transition is not universally conserved across species (Maklashina et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous comparative biochemical study.

claim: Biochemical characterization of CI from bacteria and the ciliate Tetrahymena thermophila has failed to detect a deactive state using the standard NEM approach.
source: Biochemical characterization of CI from bacteria and more recently the ciliate Tetrahymena thermophila has failed to detect a deactive state using the standard NEM approach (Maklashina et al., 2003; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous biochemical studies.

claim: T. thermophila CI's PA/MA interface is more extensive than in other species, likely precluding the opening of the complex in the same manner observed in mammals.
source: Structural analysis of the T. thermophila CI demonstrated that its PA/MA interface is more extensive than in other species (Zhou et al., 2022), likely precluding the opening of the complex in the same manner observed in mammals (Agip et al., 2018; Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020) and E. coli (Kolata and Efremov, 2021; Kravchuk et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies and represents an inference about the structural basis for biochemical differences.

claim: Fungi and metazoans diverged approximately 1300 million years ago.
source: Although fungi and metazoans diverged approximately 1300 million years ago they form a broad clade of eukaryotes known as the opisthokonts and are thus more closely related to each other than either is to the ciliate T. thermophila.
evidence: This is established evolutionary knowledge about the timing of divergence.

claim: An NEM-sensitive D-state is seen in the CI of all characterized fungi.
source: An NEM-sensitive D-state is seen in the CI of all characterized fungi but within metazoans, it is observed in deuterostomes but absent in protostomes (Figure 1A; Maklashina et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous comparative study and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Within metazoans, an NEM-sensitive D-state is observed in deuterostomes but absent in protostomes.
source: An NEM-sensitive D-state is seen in the CI of all characterized fungi but within metazoans, it is observed in deuterostomes but absent in protostomes (Figure 1A; Maklashina et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous comparative study and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Deuterostomes and protostomes diverged after the evolution of bilaterians approximately 600 million years ago.
source: Deuterostomes and protostomes diverged after the evolution of bilaterians approximately 600 million years ago (Dunn et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an evolutionary study.

claim: D. melanogaster is a genetically tractable system with a similar ETC to humans.
source: D. melanogaster is a genetically tractable system, has a similar ETC to humans, and is an emerging model for CI assembly and regulation (Garcia et al., 2017; Murari et al., 2022; Murari et al., 2021; Murari et al., 2020; Rhooms et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies using D. melanogaster as a model system.

claim: CI is an established target for insecticides and agricultural pesticides.
source: Furthermore, CI is an established target for insecticides and agricultural pesticides (Murai and Miyoshi, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review on CI as a pesticide target.

claim: Drosophila suzukii has emerged as a major pest for soft summer fruits.
source: Particularly with the emergence of Drosophila suzukii as a major pest for soft summer fruits (Tait et al., 2021), it is important to elucidate the structure of CI from a Drosophila species to identify unique aspects of CI in this genus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on D. suzukii as an agricultural pest.

claim: The D. melanogaster steady-state NADH oxidation rate is unaffected by NEM after incubation at elevated temperatures.
source: When compared to mammalian mitochondrial membranes (Sus scrofa, Figure 1C), the D. melanogaster steady-state NADH oxidation rate is unaffected by NEM after incubation at elevated temperatures (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Pre-activation with NADH sensitizes Dm-CI to NEM treatment, significantly reducing the rate of NADH oxidation after the addition of 2 mM NEM.
source: Moreover, although the addition of NADH prior to NEM rescues activity in Sus scrofa (Figure 1C), pre-activation with NADH sensitizes Dm-CI to NEM treatment, significantly reducing the rate of NADH oxidation after the addition of 2 mM NEM (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The TMH1-2ND3 cysteine remains buried in resting Dm-CI but becomes accessible during turnover.
source: This result is consistent with a model in which the TMH1-2ND3 cysteine remains buried in resting Dm-CI but becomes accessible during turnover (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2022).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data and is supported by citation to a previous mechanistic model.

claim: Exposure of the ND3 cysteine during turnover has been observed in Bos taurus CI.
source: Exposure of the ND3 cysteine during turnover has also been recently observed in Bos taurus CI (Burger et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: An activation lag phase is observed in deactivated porcine mitochondrial membranes in which the rate of NADH oxidation progressively increases until steady state turnover is achieved.
source: When the time course of NADH oxidation is examined for deactivated porcine mitochondrial membranes an activation lag phase is observed in which the rate of NADH oxidation progressively increases until steady state turnover is achieved (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: For the Porcine sample activation can be blocked by the addition of NEM or slowed by the addition of MgCl2.
source: For the Porcine sample activation can be blocked by the addition of NEM or slowed by the addition of MgCl2 (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: An activation lag phase is observed in deactivated Drosophila mitochondrial membranes.
source: In the case of deactivated Drosophila mitochondrial membranes an activation lag phase is also observed; however, the rate of activation is insensitive to the presence of either NEM or MgCl2 (Figure 1E and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and G.

claim: The rate of activation in deactivated Drosophila mitochondrial membranes is insensitive to the presence of either NEM or MgCl2.
source: In the case of deactivated Drosophila mitochondrial membranes an activation lag phase is also observed; however, the rate of activation is insensitive to the presence of either NEM or MgCl2 (Figure 1E and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and G.

claim: The activation lag is not observed after pre-activation with 5 µM of NADH in Drosophila mitochondrial membranes.
source: Importantly, the activation lag is not observed after pre-activation with 5 µM of NADH (Figure 1E and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and G.

claim: Dm-CI adopts an off-pathway resting state that is insensitive to both NEM and MgCl2.
source: These results are consistent with Dm-CI adopting an off-pathway resting state that is insensitive to both NEM and MgCl2, making it biochemically distinct from the deactive state seen in Deuterostomes and Fungi.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: NADH oxidation rates for partially purified Dm-CI were determined to be 2.87 ± 0.08 µmol NADH min–1 mg–1.
source: NADH oxidation rates for these partially purified samples were determined to be 2.87 ± 0.08 µmol NADH min–1 mg–1 (mean ± SEM, n=4) for Dm-CI and 1.77 ± 0.10 µmol NADH min–1 mg–1 (mean ± SEM, n=5) for Ss-CI prepared in the same manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of enzyme activity.

claim: NADH oxidation rates for partially purified Ss-CI were determined to be 1.77 ± 0.10 µmol NADH min–1 mg–1.
source: NADH oxidation rates for these partially purified samples were determined to be 2.87 ± 0.08 µmol NADH min–1 mg–1 (mean ± SEM, n=4) for Dm-CI and 1.77 ± 0.10 µmol NADH min–1 mg–1 (mean ± SEM, n=5) for Ss-CI prepared in the same manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of enzyme activity.

claim: Ss-CI showed a clear sensitivity to both NEM and MgCl2 in detergent-solubilized samples.
source: These data were consistent with the activity in the mitochondrial membranes in that Ss-CI showed a clear sensitivity to both NEM and MgCl2 and Dm-CI did not (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: Dm-CI did not show sensitivity to NEM and MgCl2 in detergent-solubilized samples.
source: These data were consistent with the activity in the mitochondrial membranes in that Ss-CI showed a clear sensitivity to both NEM and MgCl2 and Dm-CI did not (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: The structure of Dm-CI was resolved to a nominal resolution of 3.3 Å.
source: The structure of Dm-CI was resolved to a nominal resolution of 3.3 Å (Figure 1H, Video 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryoEM data and processing described in the methods and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Dm-CI structure contained the 14 core subunits as well as 29 accessory subunits.
source: Our Dm-CI structure contained the 14 core subunits as well as 29 accessory subunits (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), for a total composition of 43 subunits, two fewer than the 45 total subunits observed in mammals (Padavannil et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and model building.

claim: Dm-CI has a total composition of 43 subunits, two fewer than the 45 total subunits observed in mammals.
source: Our Dm-CI structure contained the 14 core subunits as well as 29 accessory subunits (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), for a total composition of 43 subunits, two fewer than the 45 total subunits observed in mammals (Padavannil et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and comparison to previous mammalian structures.

claim: The two missing subunits in Dm-CI are NDUFA2 and NDUFC1.
source: The two missing subunits are NDUFA2, and NDUFC1.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis comparing Dm-CI to mammalian CI.

claim: An accessory subunit consistent with the position of NDUFV3 in mammals was present at sub-stoichiometric levels.
source: An accessory subunit consistent with the position of NDUFV3 in mammals was present at sub-stoichiometric levels (see below).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis showing partial occupancy of the NDUFV3 site.

claim: The electron transfer pathway from FMN to the final N2 cluster was conserved in Dm-CI.
source: The electron transfer pathway from FMN to the final N2 cluster was conserved (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data showing the positions of redox cofactors.

claim: A quinone molecule was built into density in the Q-tunnel of Dm-CI.
source: Although no quinone was added to the CI preparation, we were able to build a quinone molecule into density in the Q-tunnel (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data showing density consistent with quinone.

claim: The E-channel and hydrophilic axis residues that are key to the coupling of electron transfer to proton pumping were conserved in Dm-CI.
source: The E-channel and hydrophilic axis residues that are key to the coupling of electron transfer to proton pumping were also conserved (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, H; Baradaran et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and comparison to previous structures.

claim: The metazoan-specific transmembrane accessory subunit NDUFC1 is absent from the Dm-CI structure.
source: The metazoan-specific transmembrane (TM) accessory subunit NDUFC1 is absent from the Dm-CI structure, consistent with the lack of a known ortholog (Garcia et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and citation to a previous study identifying D. melanogaster CI subunits.

claim: NDUFA2 is missing from the Dm-CI structure.
source: Conversely, the N-module subunit NDUFA2, which is seen in all other known eukaryotic CI structures (Fiedorczuk et al., 2016; Maldonado et al., 2020; Parey et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2022), is missing from the Dm-CI structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and comparison to other eukaryotic CI structures.

claim: A D. melanogaster ortholog of NDUFA2 (CG15434) has been described and is expressed in muscles.
source: A D. melanogaster ortholog of NDUFA2 (CG15434), which has a thioredoxin fold, has been described and is expressed in muscles (Garcia et al., 2017; Li et al., 2022; Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and Western blot data.

claim: The majority of a FLAG-tagged NDUFA2 transgene failed to incorporate into CI.
source: However, the majority of a FLAG-tagged NDUFA2 transgene failed to incorporate into CI ( Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, B.

claim: Density consistent with the presence of an NDUFA3 ortholog was identified in the Dm-CI structure.
source: However, we identified density consistent with the presence of an NDUFA3 ortholog (Figure 1H, Video 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data showing density at the NDUFA3 position.

claim: Amino acid assignment based on the observed side chain density allowed for the identification of an uncharacterized protein Dme1_CG9034, isoform B as the most likely NDUFA3 ortholog in D. melanogaster.
source: Amino acid assignment based on the observed side chain density allowed for the identification of an uncharacterized protein Dme1_CG9034, isoform B as the most likely NDUFA3 ortholog in D. melanogaster (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and sequence analysis.

claim: Proteomic analysis of a Dm-CI band cut from blue native gels identified CG9034 as one of the proteins that co-migrates with Dm-CI.
source: Consistent with this observation, proteomic analysis of a Dm-CI band cut from blue native gels identified CG9034 as one of the proteins that co-migrates with Dm-CI (Garcia et al., 2017); however, because it was not annotated and bioinformatics searches failed to identify it as an NDUFA3 ortholog, it was not identified as such.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous proteomic study.

claim: The loop formed by amino acid residues 665–685 of NDUFS1 forms an α-helix in other species but in Dm-CI it is a poorly resolved coil lacking secondary structure.
source: Whereas the loop formed by amino acid residues 665–685 of NDUFS1 forms an α-helix in other species, in Dm-CI it is a poorly resolved coil lacking secondary structure (Figure 2A, Video 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data comparing Dm-CI to other species.

claim: The NDUFS1 loop region forms part of the interface with accessory subunit NDUFA2 in other species.
source: This region forms part of the interface with accessory subunit NDUFA2 in other species, and the loss of the α-helix may be responsible for the absence of NDUFA2 in the Dm-CI structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on structural comparison and the absence of NDUFA2.

claim: Sequence alignment revealed that the NDUFS1 loop is four residues shorter compared to Y. lipolytica and mammals.
source: Sequence alignment revealed that this loop is four residues shorter compared to Y. lipolytica and mammals and that several bulky residues have been replaced by alanine or glycine residues in Dm-NDUFS1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) resulting in the loss of ordered secondary structure and increased flexibility.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: The helical structure in the NDUFS1 loop is not seen in bacterial CIs.
source: The helical structure in the NDUFS1 loop is not seen in bacterial CIs (Baradaran et al., 2013; Kolata and Efremov, 2021; Kravchuk et al., 2022), suggesting that this secondary structure element may have evolved in eukaryotes specifically to interact with NDUFA2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to bacterial CI structures and represents an inference about evolution.

claim: NDUFA2 knockout in HEK293T cells results in the loss of the N-module and complete loss of CI activity.
source: Whereas NDUFA2 knockout in HEK293T cells results in the loss of the N-module and complete loss of CI activity (Stroud et al., 2016), NDUFA2 knock-down in D. melanogaster has minimal effects, with CI retaining ~97% of WT (Mhc-Gal4/W1118 flies) activity during the first week after eclosing as adults (Garcia et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous functional studies in different organisms.

claim: NDUFA2 knock-down in D. melanogaster has minimal effects, with CI retaining ~97% of WT activity during the first week after eclosing as adults.
source: Whereas NDUFA2 knockout in HEK293T cells results in the loss of the N-module and complete loss of CI activity (Stroud et al., 2016), NDUFA2 knock-down in D. melanogaster has minimal effects, with CI retaining ~97% of WT (Mhc-Gal4/W1118 flies) activity during the first week after eclosing as adults (Garcia et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous functional study in D. melanogaster.

claim: NDUFA2 only interacts with NDUFS1.
source: Given that NDUFA2 only interacts with NDUFS1, it was proposed that NDUFA2 binding compensates for truncation of NDUFS1's 'D domain' that is otherwise present in bacterial orthologs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C; Padavannil et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and citation to a previous proposal.

claim: Domain D remains short in Dm-NDUFS1 like other eukaryotes.
source: However, like other eukaryotes, domain D remains short in Dm-NDUFS1 and the reason for the sustained stability of Dm-CI when NDUFA2 is knocked down is unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and represents an observation about an unresolved question.

claim: NDUFS7 in D. melanogaster has an extended N-terminus relative to mammalian CI, as in Y. lipolytica.
source: As in Y. lipolytica, NDUFS7 in D. melanogaster has an extended N-terminus relative to mammalian CI (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The N-terminus of Dm-NDUFS7 is flipped ~180° relative to Yl-NDUFS7, binding overtop of NDUFA12 instead of along the surface of NDUFA9.
source: However, whereas the N-terminus of Yl-NDUFS7 binds along the surface of NDUFA9, that of Dm-CI is flipped ~180° binding overtop of NDUFA12 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The additional interface between NDUFS7 and NDUFA12 would stabilize the association of NDUFA12 in Dm-CI.
source: This additional interface would stabilize the association of NDUFA12 in Dm-CI.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation of additional interactions.

claim: During CI assembly, the assembly factor NDUFAF2 binds at the equivalent position of NDUFA12 and is exchanged for NDUFA12 before the full assembly of the PA.
source: During CI assembly, the assembly factor NDUFAF2 binds at the equivalent position of NDUFA12 (Parey et al., 2019) and is exchanged for NDUFA12 before the full assembly of the PA (Andrews et al., 2013; Vogel et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous assembly studies.

claim: The additional interactions between NDUFS7 and NDUFA12 in Dm-CI may influence the assembly of the PA by promoting the exchange of NDUFAF2 with NDUFA12 through the stabilization of NDUFA12 binding.
source: The additional interactions between NDUFS7 and NDUFA12 in Dm-CI may thus influence the assembly of the PA by promoting the exchange of NDUFAF2 with NDUFA12 through the stabilization of NDUFA12 binding (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data and knowledge of assembly pathways.

claim: Dm-ND2 lacks three TMHs at the N-terminus, thus having 11 TMHs as opposed to the 14 TMHs otherwise seen in bacteria, plants, ciliates, and yeast.
source: As in mammalian CI, Dm-ND2 lacks three TMHs at the N-terminus, thus having 11 TMHs as opposed to the 14 TMHs otherwise seen in bacteria, plants, ciliates, and yeast (Birrell and Hirst, 2010; Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and citation to a previous comparative study.

claim: The cavity formed by the lack of the three TMHs in ND2 is filled with lipids that are held in place in part by the NDUFC2 subunit.
source: The cavity formed by the lack of the three TMHs is filled with lipids that are held in place in part by the NDUFC2 subunit (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data showing lipid binding.

claim: The last TMH in Dm-ND2 (TMH11ND2) has two additional turns compared to TMH11ND2 of mammals.
source: Similar to other eukaryotic CIs, the last TMH in Dm-ND2 (TMH11ND2), has two additional turns, compared to TMH11ND2 of mammals (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B; Klusch et al., 2021; Parey et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data and citations.

claim: It has been proposed that in mammals, subunit NDUFC1 plays a role in shortening TMH11ND2 by binding a cardiolipin molecule that caps the helix stabilizing its partially unwound state.
source: It has been proposed that in mammals, subunit NDUFC1 plays a role in shortening TMH11ND2 by binding a cardiolipin molecule that caps the helix stabilizing its partially unwound state (Padavannil et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous proposal.

claim: D. melanogaster lacks accessory subunit NDUFC1 and has a longer TMH11ND2 relative to mammals, supporting the proposed role of NDUFC1 in mammals.
source: Given that D. melanogaster lacks accessory subunit NDUFC1 and has a longer TMH11ND2 relative to mammals, this supports the proposed role of NDUFC1 in mammals.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison supporting a previous hypothesis.

claim: Lack of NDUFC1 in Dm-CI indicates that it was recruited as an accessory subunit only after the split of Protostomia and Deuterostomia.
source: Lack of NDUFC1 in Dm-CI also indicates that it was recruited as an accessory subunit only after the split of Protostomia and Deuterostomia.
evidence: This is an inference about evolution based on the absence of NDUFC1 in Dm-CI.

claim: In both mammals and D. melanogaster, the TMH10-11ND2 loop provides a major interface with the metazoan-specific subunit NDUFA10.
source: In both mammals and D. melanogaster, the TMH10-11ND2 loop provides a major interface with the metazoan-specific subunit NDUFA10 (Figure 2E and Video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: In Y. lipolytica, which lacks any subunit binding on the matrix side of ND2, the TMH10-11ND2 loop spans across the matrix surface of ND2 as a coil.
source: In Y. lipolytica, which lacks any subunit binding on the matrix side of ND2, as well as in plants and Tetrahymena which use the equivalent loop to interact with their γ-carbonic anhydrase subunit (Klusch et al., 2021; Maldonado et al., 2020; Soufari et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2022), the TMH10-11ND2 loop spans across the matrix surface of ND2 as a coil.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: In mammals, TMH10-11ND2 spans the same distance across the matrix surface but forms a short α-helix that interacts directly with NDUFA10.
source: In mammals, TMH10-11ND2 spans the same distance across the matrix surface but forms a short α-helix that interacts directly with NDUFA10 (Figure 2D and E and Video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: The length of the TMH10-11ND2 loop is only shorter by two residues in D. melanogaster compared to mammals.
source: Given that the length of the TMH10-11ND2 loop is only shorter by two residues in D. melanogaster compared to mammals (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), the additional residues required for the TMH10-11ND2 loop to fold into an α-helix in mammals must come from the unwinding of TMH11ND2.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: The additional residues required for the TMH10-11ND2 loop to fold into an α-helix in mammals must come from the unwinding of TMH11ND2.
source: Given that the length of the TMH10-11ND2 loop is only shorter by two residues in D. melanogaster compared to mammals (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), the additional residues required for the TMH10-11ND2 loop to fold into an α-helix in mammals must come from the unwinding of TMH11ND2.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and sequence comparison.

claim: The mammalian interface between ND2 and NDUFA10 cannot form before NDUFC1 binds and recruits a cardiolipin to partially unwind TMH11ND2.
source: Thus, a simple model emerges for how mammalian CI is dependent on NDUFC1 for assembly. Namely, the mammalian interface between ND2 and NDUFA10 cannot form before NDUFC1 binds and recruits a cardiolipin to partially unwind TMH11ND2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C; Padavannil et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on structural inference and citation to previous work.

claim: This model is consistent with the known binding order and dependencies of NDUFC1 and NDUFA10 to ND2 during CI assembly.
source: This model is consistent with the known binding order and dependencies of NDUFC1 and NDUFA10 to ND2 during CI assembly (Guerrero-Castillo et al., 2017; Stroud et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous assembly studies.

claim: In Dm-CI, due to an extended C-terminal coil, the MA accessory subunit NDUFA11 has much more extensive interaction with the core subunits than seen in mammals.
source: In Dm-CI, due to an extended C-terminal coil, the MA accessory subunit NDUFA11 has much more extensive interaction with the core subunits than seen in mammals (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A and B and Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: In mammalian CI, only limited protein-protein contacts between NDUFA11 and other CI subunits are observed, dominated mainly by its short C-terminal coil.
source: In mammalian CI, only limited protein-protein contacts between NDUFA11 and other CI subunits are observed, dominated mainly by its short C-terminal coil (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from mammalian CI.

claim: Detergent extraction can result in the loss of NDUFA11 in mammals, resulting in so-called 'state 3' particles.
source: For this reason, detergent extraction can result in the loss of NDUFA11 in mammals, resulting in so-called 'state 3' particles (Chung et al., 2022b; Fiedorczuk et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: In the fungus Y. lipolytica the C-terminus of NDUFA11 is much longer and extends along the matrix side of the complex.
source: However, in the fungus Y. lipolytica the C-terminus of NDUFA11 is much longer and extends along the matrix side of the complex (Parey et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous structural study.

claim: NDUFA11 in Y. lipolytica is harder to dissociate from the complex even after treatment with harsh detergents.
source: Likely for this reason NDUFA11 in Y. lipolytica is harder to dissociate from the complex even after treatment with harsh detergents (Angerer et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous biochemical study and represents an inference about the structural basis.

claim: The C-terminus of Dm-NDUFA11 runs across the membrane arm, tucking between NDUFB5, NDUFS5, NDUFA8, and ND2, emerging adjacent to NDUFC2 on the opposite side.
source: However, unlike the C-terminus in Y. lipolytica NDUFA11 which runs along the length of the MA, that of Dm-NDUFA11 runs across the membrane arm (i.e. perpendicular to the long axis), tucking between NDUFB5, NDUFS5, NDUFA8, and ND2, emerging adjacent to NDUFC2 on the opposite side (Figure 2F and Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: This arrangement of Dm-NDUFA11 is not seen in any other known CI structure.
source: This arrangement is not seen in any other known CI structure.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on knowledge of other CI structures.

claim: The C-terminus of Dm-NDUFA11 occupies space that is occupied by subunit NDUX1 (NUXM) in yeast, plants, and ciliates.
source: The C-terminus of Dm-NDUFA11 occupies space that is occupied by subunit NDUX1 (NUXM) in yeast, plants, and ciliates (a subunit that is lost in metazoans along with the truncation of ND2), and the N-terminus of NDUFC2 in mammals (Fiedorczuk et al., 2016; Klusch et al., 2021; Maldonado et al., 2020; Parey et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison and citations.

claim: Mammalian CI is assembled through a series of intermediates and NDUFA11 is a terminally associated protein that does not form a part of any assembly intermediate.
source: Mammalian CI is assembled through a series of intermediates and NDUFA11 is a terminally associated protein that does not form a part of any assembly intermediate (Guerrero-Castillo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous assembly study.

claim: In mammals, NDUFB5, NDUFB8, and NDUFS5 on the IMS side are all present in assembly intermediates prior to the addition of NDUFA11.
source: Also in mammals, NDUFB5, NDUFB8, and NDUFS5 on the IMS side are all present in assembly intermediates prior to the addition of NDUFA11 (Guerrero-Castillo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous assembly study.

claim: The arrangement seen in Dm-CI suggests that Dm-NDUFA11 would need to bind Dm-ND2 before Dm-NDUFB5, Dm-NDUFA8, and Dm-NDUFS5.
source: The arrangement seen in Dm-CI, in which the C-terminus of Dm-NDUFA11 is sandwiched between Dm-NDUFB5, Dm-NDUFA8, Dm-NDUFS5, and Dm-ND2 (Video 5), suggests that Dm-NDUFA11 would need to bind Dm-ND2 before Dm-NDUFB5, Dm-NDUFA8, and Dm-NDUFS5.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data about assembly order.

claim: ND5 would need to associate with ND2 before NDUA11 could bind because NDUFA11 binds on top of ND5-HL.
source: However, as NDUFA11 binds on top of ND5-HL, ND5 would need to associate with ND2 before NDUA11 could bind.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data about assembly order.

claim: This order of events is counter to what occurs in mammals and indicates that assembly of this region of Dm-CI might proceed via a distinct mechanism than that of mammals.
source: This order of events is counter to what occurs in mammals (Guerrero-Castillo et al., 2017) and indicates that like plant CI (Ligas et al., 2018), assembly of this region of Dm-CI might proceed via a distinct mechanism than that of mammals.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison and citations to assembly studies.

claim: In mammals there are two isoforms of the NDFUV3 subunit – a long isoform NDUFV3-L and a short isoform NDUFV3-S.
source: In mammals there are two isoforms of the NDFUV3 subunit – a long isoform NDUFV3-L and a short isoform NDUFV3-S – and it has been proposed that binding of the different isoforms may impact the activity of CI (Bridges et al., 2016; Dibley et al., 2017; Guerrero-Castillo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It has been proposed that binding of the different NDUFV3 isoforms may impact the activity of CI.
source: In mammals there are two isoforms of the NDFUV3 subunit – a long isoform NDUFV3-L and a short isoform NDUFV3-S – and it has been proposed that binding of the different isoforms may impact the activity of CI (Bridges et al., 2016; Dibley et al., 2017; Guerrero-Castillo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies proposing this regulatory mechanism.

claim: Density for a subunit at the position of NDUFV3 in mammals was observed in the Dm-CI structure.
source: Density for a subunit at the position of NDUFV3 in mammals was also observed in the Dm-CI structure (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: In the average structure calculated using all Dm-CI particles, the NDUFV3 density was weak compared to that of the surrounding core subunits.
source: However, in the average structure calculated using all Dm-CI particles, this density was weak compared to that of the surrounding core subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data analysis.

claim: When focused refinements were performed with a mask around the tip of the PA, two clear classes could be isolated differing in the occupancy of the NDUFV3 site.
source: When focused refinements were performed with a mask around the tip of the PA, two clear classes could be isolated differing in the occupancy of the NDUFV3 site (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryoEM data processing and classification.

claim: In Dm-CI the NDUFV3 site is only partially occupied.
source: Thus, in Dm-CI this site is only partially occupied.
evidence: This is an inference based on the classification showing different occupancy states.

claim: The 68 kDa fragment of the atypical cadherin (Ft4) can regulate Dm-CI activity.
source: The 68 kDa fragment of the atypical cadherin (Ft4) can regulate Dm-CI activity (Sing et al., 2014) and it was proposed that it may bind to Dm-CI at the NDUFV3 site (Bridges et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: It was proposed that Ft4 may bind to Dm-CI at the NDUFV3 site.
source: The 68 kDa fragment of the atypical cadherin (Ft4) can regulate Dm-CI activity (Sing et al., 2014) and it was proposed that it may bind to Dm-CI at the NDUFV3 site (Bridges et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous proposal.

claim: The results are consistent with the hypothesis that binding at the NDUFV3 site may be regulatory.
source: The density of the occupied class was too noisy to confidently assign the sequence of the subunit from the map (Figure 3A). However, our results are consistent with the hypothesis that binding at this site may be regulatory (Bridges et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data supporting a previous hypothesis.

claim: In mammals NDUFA10 forms a state-dependent interface with accessory subunit NDUFA5.
source: In addition to the major interface between NDUFA10 and ND2, in mammals NDUFA10 forms a state-dependent interface with accessory subunit NDUFA5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A; Agip et al., 2018; Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Letts et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: In Dm-CI, the interface between NDUFA10 and NDUFA5 is larger due to an extended NDUFA10 N-terminal coil that inserts between NDUFA10 and NDUFA5.
source: In Dm-CI, the interface between NDUFA10 and NDUFA5 is larger due to an extended NDUFA10 N-terminal coil that inserts between NDUFA10 and NDUFA5 (Figure 3B and C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: The enhanced interface between Dm-NDUFA10 and Dm-NDUFA5 would make these subunits more difficult to separate.
source: The enhanced interface between Dm-NDUFA10 and Dm-NDUFA5 would make these subunits more difficult to separate and indicates that, although the interactions at this interface may be state-dependent (see below), the interface is less likely to be fully broken as seen in the mammalian context (Agip et al., 2018; Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Letts et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data.

claim: In mammals, the N-terminus of NDUFB4 forms part of the only matrix interface between CI and CIII2 in SC I+III2.
source: In mammals, the N-terminus of NDUFB4 forms part of the only matrix interface between CI and CIII2 in SC I+III2 (Letts et al., 2019; Letts and Sazanov, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies of supercomplexes.

claim: In this interaction, a loop from the UQRC1 subunit of one CIII protomer binds in between the N-terminus of NDUFB4 and the three-helix-bundle of subunit NDUFB9.
source: In this interaction, a loop from the UQRC1 subunit of one CIII protomer binds in between the N-terminus of NDUFB4 and the three-helix-bundle of subunit NDUFB9.
evidence: This claim is supported by knowledge of supercomplex structures.

claim: In Dm-CI the N-terminus of Dm-NDUFB4 is truncated relative to that of mammals and does not extend far enough towards NDUFB9 to form this interface.
source: In Dm-CI the N-terminus of Dm-NDUFB4 is truncated relative to that of mammals and does not extend far enough towards NDUFB9 to form this interface (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The lack of the NDUFB4-CIII2 interface likely contributes to the observed low abundance of SCs in D. melanogaster mitochondria.
source: Thus, the lack of this interface likely contributes to the observed low abundance of SCs in D. melanogaster mitochondria.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data explaining a biochemical observation.

claim: It has been proposed that NDUFA11's interaction with CI may have been weakened in species, such as mammals, to promote SC formation by requiring the presence of CIII2 to hold NDUFA11 in place.
source: Additionally, given its role in bridging between CI and CIII2 in respiratory SCs (Letts et al., 2019; Letts and Sazanov, 2017), it has been proposed that NDUFA11's interaction with CI may have been weakened in species, such as mammals, to promote SC formation by requiring the presence of CIII2 to hold NDUFA11 in place (Padavannil et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and a proposal.

claim: The extended interaction interface provided by the C-terminus of Dm-NDUFA11 indicates that Dm-NDUFA11 is not dependent on the presence of CIII2 for its stable association with the Dm-CI.
source: The extended interaction interface provided by the C-terminus of Dm-NDUFA11 indicates that Dm-NDUFA11 is not dependent on the presence of CIII2 for its stable association with the Dm-CI.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data.

claim: The Dm-CI structure supports the proposed inverse relationship between the strength of the interaction between NDUFA11 and CI and the abundance of SCs.
source: Thus, the Dm-CI structure supports the proposed inverse relationship between the strength of the interaction between NDUFA11 and CI and the abundance of SCs (Padavannil et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data supporting a previous proposal.

claim: Lipids form an integral part of the CI MA and loss of lipids during purification results in diminished CI activity.
source: Lipids form an integral part of the CI MA and loss of lipids during purification results in diminished CI activity (Letts et al., 2016a; Padavannil et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Across species, structural lipids are seen tightly binding to the surface of CI at the interface of the core H+-pumping subunits.
source: Across species, structural lipids are seen tightly binding to the surface of CI at the interface of the core H+-pumping subunits and specific deformation of the lipid membrane by NDUFA9 occurs adjacent to the Q-tunnel (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Parey et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Specific deformation of the lipid membrane by NDUFA9 occurs adjacent to the Q-tunnel.
source: Across species, structural lipids are seen tightly binding to the surface of CI at the interface of the core H+-pumping subunits and specific deformation of the lipid membrane by NDUFA9 occurs adjacent to the Q-tunnel (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Parey et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The pattern of lipid binding to Dm-CI is like that seen in other CI structures with two notable exceptions.
source: In general, the pattern of lipid binding to Dm-CI (Figure 1—figure supplement 4I) is like that seen in other CI structures with two notable exceptions.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison.

claim: Dm-ND5 lacks the first TMH for a total of only 15 TMHs instead of 16 TMHs observed in ND5 of Y. lipolytica and mammals.
source: First, instead of 16 TMHs observed in ND5 of Y. lipolytica and mammals, Dm-ND5 lacks the first TMH for a total of only 15 (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: The region occupied by ND5-TMH1 in other species is not occupied by any other protein subunit but binds lipid in Dm-CI.
source: Like what is seen with the metazoan-specific shortening of ND2 discussed above, the region occupied by ND5-TMH1 in other species is not occupied by any other protein subunit but binds lipid (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: Loss of the first TMH of ND5 must have occurred after the split of Protostomia and Deuterostomia because mammalian ND5 maintains its full complement of helices.
source: As mammalian ND5 maintains its full complement of helices, loss of the first TMH must have occurred after the split of Protostomia and Deuterostomia, but how widespread the ND5 deletion is in Protostomia along with any functional implications remains to be determined.
evidence: This is an inference about evolution based on structural comparison.

claim: In mammals, the N-terminus of the two-TMH accessory subunit NDUFC2 binds underneath ND2 in the pocket left by the deletion of the first three ND2 TMHs.
source: Second, in mammals, the N-terminus of the two-TMH accessory subunit NDUFC2 binds underneath ND2 in the pocket left by the deletion of the first three ND2 TMHs.
evidence: This claim is supported by knowledge of mammalian CI structure.

claim: In Dm-CI the space under ND2 is filled by the C-terminus of NDUFA11.
source: However, in Dm-CI this space is filled by the C-terminus of NDUFA11 (Figure 2C and Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: Dm-NDUFC2 has an extended N-terminus relative to that of Y. lipolytica.
source: Like mammalian NDUFC2, Dm-NDUFC2 has an extended N-terminus relative to that of Y. lipolytica (Figure 2C and Figure 3—figure supplement 5A); however, instead of crossing over TMH2C2 and binding under ND2, it crosses over the C-terminal coil of NDUFA8 and forms additional interactions with NDUFB1 and NDUFB5 (Figure 2C and Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The N-terminus of Dm-NDUFC2 crosses over the C-terminal coil of NDUFA8 and forms additional interactions with NDUFB1 and NDUFB5.
source: Like mammalian NDUFC2, Dm-NDUFC2 has an extended N-terminus relative to that of Y. lipolytica (Figure 2C and Figure 3—figure supplement 5A); however, instead of crossing over TMH2C2 and binding under ND2, it crosses over the C-terminal coil of NDUFA8 and forms additional interactions with NDUFB1 and NDUFB5 (Figure 2C and Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: These additional interactions of Dm-NDUFC2 contribute to lipid binding at the ND2/ND4 interface by capping this pocket.
source: These additional interactions contribute to lipid binding at the ND2/ND4 interface by capping this pocket and likely help to stabilize lipid binding at the interface between the two H+-pumping core subunits.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data about the functional role of these interactions.

claim: Focused classifications using a mask encompassing subunits NDUFA10, NDUFA5, NDUFA6, and NDUFAB1-α revealed two major classes and two minor classes of Dm-CI particles.
source: This classification revealed two major classes and two minor classes of Dm-CI particles that differ in the presence of an ordered α-helical element from NDUFS4 bound at the interface of NDUFA5, NDUFA10, and NDUFA6 and in the angle between the PA and MA (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryoEM data processing and classification.

claim: The classes differ in the presence of an ordered α-helical element from NDUFS4 bound at the interface of NDUFA5, NDUFA10, and NDUFA6 and in the angle between the PA and MA.
source: This classification revealed two major classes and two minor classes of Dm-CI particles that differ in the presence of an ordered α-helical element from NDUFS4 bound at the interface of NDUFA5, NDUFA10, and NDUFA6 and in the angle between the PA and MA (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryoEM data processing and classification.

claim: Only in one of the major classes is the NDUFS4 helix visible, while in the other major class and two minor classes this helix is disordered.
source: Only in one of the major classes is the NDUFS4 helix visible, while in the other major class and two minor classes this helix is disordered.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from classification.

claim: The states are named the NDUFS4-helix-locked (helix-locked) state and the flexible class 1-3 states.
source: We name the states the NDUFS4-helix-locked (helix-locked) state and the flexible class 1-3 states (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a naming convention established by the authors based on structural features.

claim: The name helix-locked state refers to the fact that the positions of the PA and MA are 'locked' relative to each other due to the presence of the NDUFS4 helix.
source: The name helix-locked state refers to the fact that the positions of the PA and MA are 'locked' relative to each other due to the presence of the NDUFS4 helix (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an explanation of the naming convention based on structural interpretation.

claim: In the absence of the lock helix, the relative positions of PA and MA vary and thus the complex is more flexible.
source: In the absence of the lock helix, the relative positions of PA and MA vary and thus the complex is more flexible (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Kravchuk et al., 2022; Parey et al., 2021) as indicated by the three distinct sub-classes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data and citations to previous studies.

claim: 3DVA performed on the full set of particles revealed a smooth transition between the flexible sub-states along with the disappearance of the NDUFS4 helical density.
source: Three-dimensional variability analysis (3DVA) performed on the full set of particles revealed a smooth transition between the flexible sub-states along with the disappearance of the NDUFS4 helical density (Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3DVA computational analysis of cryoEM data.

claim: Frozen Dm-CI particles adopt conformations along the trajectory from the major flexible class 1 state towards the helix-locked state.
source: This indicates that the frozen Dm-CI particles adopt conformations along the trajectory from the major flexible class 1 state, which is the furthest rotated relative to the helix-locked state, towards the helix-locked state.
evidence: This is an inference based on 3DVA analysis.

claim: Once the PA and MA are positioned such that they are far enough apart to accommodate the NDUFS4 helix, the binding of the helix 'locks' their relative positions.
source: Once the PA and MA are positioned such that they are far enough apart to accommodate the NDUFS4 helix, the binding of the helix 'locks' their relative positions (Figure 4A and Video 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data about the mechanism of locking.

claim: The N-terminal region of NDUFS4 that forms the lock helix is not conserved in Y. lipolytica or mammals.
source: The N-terminal region of NDUFS4 that forms the lock helix is not conserved in Y. lipolytica or mammals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) suggesting that it evolved after the split of Protostomia and Deuterostomia.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence comparison data.

claim: The NDUFS4 lock helix evolved after the split of Protostomia and Deuterostomia.
source: The N-terminal region of NDUFS4 that forms the lock helix is not conserved in Y. lipolytica or mammals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) suggesting that it evolved after the split of Protostomia and Deuterostomia.
evidence: This is an inference about evolution based on sequence comparison.

claim: The helix-locked state and the flexible class 1 state mainly differ from each other by a rotation of the PA and the tilting of subunit ND1.
source: Overall, the helix-locked state and the flexible class 1 state mainly differ from each other by a rotation of the PA and the tilting of subunit ND1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The rotation and angle between the PA and MA in the Dm-CI states do not correspond to those seen in any of the mammalian states but are more like states seen in E. coli CI and the hyper thermophilic fungus Chaetomium thermophilum.
source: The rotation and angle between the PA and MA in the Dm-CI states do not correspond to those seen in any of the mammalian states but are more like states seen in E. coli CI and the hyper thermophilic fungus Chaetomium thermophilum (Figure 4—figure supplement 4; Kravchuk et al., 2022; Laube et al., 2022a).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison and citations.

claim: Across species there is not a clear one-to-one mapping of the observed states indicating that the relative positions of the PA and MA are not indicative of conserved functional states of the complex.
source: However, as has been recently acknowledged (Kravchuk et al., 2022), across species there is not a clear one-to-one mapping of the observed states indicating that the relative positions of the PA and MA are not indicative of conserved functional states of the complex as initially proposed (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent acknowledgment in the literature.

claim: According to the measure of distance between the center of mass of NDUFAB1-α and that of NDUFA10, the helix-locked state is most like the closed/active states.
source: According to this measure, the helix-locked state is most like the closed/active states (Figure 4—figure supplement 5) and the Dm-CI flexible class 1 state is most like the open/deactive states of mammalian CI (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison using a specific metric.

claim: The Dm-CI flexible class 1 state is most like the open/deactive states of mammalian CI according to the distance between the center of mass of NDUFAB1-α and that of NDUFA10.
source: According to this measure, the helix-locked state is most like the closed/active states (Figure 4—figure supplement 5) and the Dm-CI flexible class 1 state is most like the open/deactive states of mammalian CI (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison using a specific metric.

claim: The position of NDUFAB1-α in flexible class 1 is consistent with the formation of salt-bridges between residues D146AB1-α, D149AB1-α and R209A10.
source: Although the density of the NDUFAB1-α subunit is weak due to flexibility, its position in flexible class 1 is consistent with the formation of salt-bridges between residues D146AB1-α, D149AB1-α and R209A10 (Figure 4B and Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and modeling of interactions.

claim: In plant and Tetrahymena CI, the NDUFAB1-α subunit is involved in bridging interactions between the PA and MA.
source: In plant and Tetrahymena CI, the NDUFAB1-α subunit is involved in bridging interactions between the PA and MA (Klusch et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2022); however, to our knowledge, this is the first indication of direct bridging between the PA and MA via NDUFA10 and NDUFAB1-α in any metazoan structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: This is the first indication of direct bridging between the PA and MA via NDUFA10 and NDUFAB1-α in any metazoan structure.
source: In plant and Tetrahymena CI, the NDUFAB1-α subunit is involved in bridging interactions between the PA and MA (Klusch et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2022); however, to our knowledge, this is the first indication of direct bridging between the PA and MA via NDUFA10 and NDUFAB1-α in any metazoan structure.
evidence: This is a claim about novelty based on comparison to previous structures.

claim: NDUFA5 and NDUFA10 remain in direct contact in both the helix-locked and the flexible states.
source: Although NDUFA5 and NDUFA10 remain in direct contact in both the helix-locked and the flexible states, there is a state-dependent change in their interaction (Figure 4 and Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: There is a state-dependent change in the interaction between NDUFA5 and NDUFA10.
source: Although NDUFA5 and NDUFA10 remain in direct contact in both the helix-locked and the flexible states, there is a state-dependent change in their interaction (Figure 4 and Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: In the helix-locked state, the interaction between NDUFA5 and NDUFA10 is mediated in part by the N-terminus of NDUFS4 which binds along the surface of NDUFA10; and D34S4 forms a salt bridge with R92A5.
source: In the helix-locked state, the interaction between NDUFA5 and NDUFA10 is mediated in part by the N-terminus of NDUFS4 which binds along the surface of NDUFA10; and D34S4 forms a salt bridge with R92A5 (Figure 4A and Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data showing specific interactions.

claim: In the flexible class 1 state, the N-terminus of NDUFS4 is disordered, and NDUFA5 slides along the surface of NDUFA10 such that R92A5 forms a salt bridge with E302A10.
source: In the flexible class 1 state, the N-terminus of NDUFS4 is disordered, and NDUFA5 slides along the surface of NDUFA10 such that R92A5 forms a salt bridge with E302A10 (Figure 4B and Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data showing specific interactions.

claim: R92A5 is used to form salt bridging interactions with NDUFS4 and NDUFA10 in a state-dependent manner.
source: Thus, R92A5 is used to form salt bridging interactions with NDUFS4 and NDUFA10 in a state-dependent manner (Figure 4 and Video 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data about the role of this residue.

claim: Conformational changes in loops adjacent to the CoQ reduction site were seen between the helix-locked and flexible class 1 states of Dm-CI.
source: Conformational changes in loops adjacent to the CoQ reduction site were seen between the helix-locked and flexible class 1 states of Dm-CI (Figure 5 and Video 7).
